---
format: gfm
title: Measles wastewater surveillance with epiworldR
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)
for (f in list.files("R", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)
res <- readRDS("analysis/results.rds")
p   <- res[["0"]]$params
fmt <- function(x, d = 0) {
  x <- round(x, d)
  formatC(x + 0, format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",") # + 0 drops -0
}
```

This project simulates measles outbreaks in a synthetic city of `r fmt(p$n)`
people and compares three scenarios:

1. **Baseline**: the outbreak runs with no surveillance-triggered
   intervention.
2. **Wastewater (WW)**: wastewater is sampled three times a week, results are
   available after a lab turnaround time, and an intervention starts once a
   result reaches a threshold.
3. **Cases**: each case is detected during its rash period with probability
   `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`% and reported after a delay, and the same
   intervention starts once cumulative reported cases reach a threshold.
   Clinical detection of measles is far from perfect, so we vary this
   probability in a sensitivity analysis (see
   [Case detection probability](#case-detection-probability)).

The intervention reduces the non-household contacts (school, work, and other
settings) of school-age groups (5–19) by `r 100 * p$school_contact_reduction`%
for the rest of the outbreak. The WW threshold is calibrated so both triggers
respond to the same number of cases; the difference between them is *when*
each system sees those cases.

## Model

### Population and contacts

- **Disease model**: `measles::ModelMeaslesMixing()` (latent, prodromal, rash,
  hospitalized, recovered), with one entity per 5-year age group (0–4, …,
  75+). Individual-level isolation, quarantine, and contact tracing are off in
  every scenario, so the only response is the triggered intervention.
- **Age distribution**: Salt Lake County, UT (2025 Census estimates, via the
  [multigroup.vaccine](https://github.com/EpiForeSITE/multigroup-vaccine)
  package), rescaled to `r fmt(p$n)` people.
- **Contacts**: the setting-specific (household, school, work, other)
  contact matrices from
  [Epistorm-Mix](https://github.com/epistorm/Epistorm-Mix) (see
  [data/epistorm](data/epistorm/README.md)), re-weighted to the county's age
  distribution and made reciprocal with `measles::make_cmat_symmetric()`.
- **Transmission**: the contact matrix is scaled to R0 = `r p$R0` (a
  parameter), first analytically and then by simulation, because the
  agent-based model realizes a lower R0 than the analytic formula. The
  simulated R0 is `r fmt(res[["0"]]$R0_sim, 2)`. Under the intervention it
  drops to about `r fmt(res[["0"]]$R_int, 1)`; school-age contacts outside the
  home account for only part of transmission.
- **Natural history**: `r p$incubation_period` days latent, `r p$prodromal_period`
  days prodromal, and `r p$rash_period` days of rash. That puts rash onset
  about 14 days after infection and makes people infectious from 4 days
  before to 4 days after rash onset. People with rash keep
  `r 100 * (1 - p$rash_reduction_contact_rate)`% of their contacts. 20% are
  hospitalized.

### Wastewater shedding

The shedding model follows the structure of the CDC
[wwinference](https://github.com/CDCgov/ww-inference-model) model. The
expected concentration on day $t$ is

$$
C(t) = \frac{1}{\alpha N} \sum_{\tau=0}^{\tau_{end}} s(\tau)\, G(t - \tau),
$$

where $G(d)$ is the total number of genome copies shed by the people whose
prodrome started on day $d$, $\alpha$ is the wastewater volume per person per
day, and $N$ is the population. The shedding profile $s(\tau)$ is
piecewise linear on the log10 scale: it rises to its peak at $\tau_{peak}$
and declines back to zero at $\tau_{end}$, normalized to sum to one. Two
changes from the COVID model:

- $\tau$ is counted from **prodrome onset**, not infection, because measles RNA
  appears in urine during the prodrome and peaks around rash onset.
- Each person's total shedding is drawn from a log-normal distribution, since
  measured measles shedding varies over four orders of magnitude.

Measurements are log-normal around $C(t)$ and recorded as non-detects below
the limit of detection (LOD).

| Parameter | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Peak shedding, days after prodrome onset ($\tau_{peak}$) | `r p$ww_t_peak` (rash onset) | Prodromal and rash-onset shedding (Corchis-Scott et al. 2026) |
| End of shedding ($\tau_{end}$) | `r p$ww_t_end` (≈14 days after rash) | Urine RNA up to 14 days (Corchis-Scott et al. 2026); RT-PCR positive up to 10+ days after rash (CDC) |
| Peak-to-tail ratio (log10) | `r p$ww_log10_vpeak` | Assumption (shape only; profile is normalized) |
| Copies per infection, log10 mean (SD) | `r p$ww_log10_g_mean` (`r p$ww_log10_g_sd`) | ≈10^8.7 copies/infection/day over ≈2 weeks (STOTEN 2024 model); median 1.4×10^11 copies/person/day, 4 orders of magnitude range (Corchis-Scott et al. 2026) |
| Wastewater per person per day ($\alpha$) | `r fmt(p$ww_alpha)` mL | wwinference (Ortiz 2024) |
| Measurement SD (log scale) | `r p$ww_sigma` | Assumption |
| LOD | `r p$ww_lod` copies/mL (3 log10 copies/L) | Process LOD in STOTEN 2024 |
| Sampling | 3 times a week | Ontario (Corchis-Scott et al. 2026) |
| Lab turnaround | `r p$ww_lab_delay` days (sensitivity 0–7) | Assumption |
| Case detection probability (during rash) | `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`% (sensitivity `r paste0(100 * sort(unique(res[[1]]$report_prob$case_report_prob)), collapse = ", ")`%) | Assumption; Ontario estimated 5–10× under-reporting |
| Case reporting delay | `r p$case_report_delay` days after rash onset | Assumption |
| Case trigger | `r p$trigger_cases` cumulative reported cases | Assumption |

With these values, one person with median shedding, on their peak day, in a
city of `r fmt(p$n)`
produces a concentration near the LOD, roughly in line with the
STOTEN 2024 estimate that about 8 cases per 10,000 people are needed for 50%
detection.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kernel
#| fig-cap: "Shedding profile, relative to prodrome onset. The dashed line marks rash onset."
#| fig-height: 3
k <- shedding_kernel(p$ww_t_peak, p$ww_t_end, p$ww_log10_vpeak)
ggplot(data.frame(tau = seq_along(k) - 1, s = k), aes(tau, s)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = p$prodromal_period, linetype = 2) +
  labs(x = "Days since prodrome onset", y = "Share of total shedding") +
  theme_minimal()
```

### Calibrating the triggers

The clinical system sees a case at rash onset, but only after the reporting
delay. WW sees it from the prodrome, but only after the lab turnaround. The
WW threshold is calibrated on the baseline runs so that, at the median, both
triggers fire after the same number of cases:

- **Cases**: cumulative rash onsets on the rash day of the report that crosses
  the case threshold.
- **WW**: cumulative prodrome onsets on the collection day of the first sample
  above the WW threshold.

Both medians are taken over the same runs, those where the case trigger fires.
If WW never crosses the threshold in one of those runs, it counts as WW never
seeing the outbreak, so a threshold cannot look well calibrated just by
missing the outbreaks it would detect late. The calibration uses the
reference case detection probability (`r 100 * p$case_report_prob`%).

Because runs with the same seed share their trajectory until the trigger, the
scenarios are paired, and the lead time is the case trigger day minus the WW
trigger day in the same outbreak.

## Results

Each scenario was simulated 400 times (`analysis/run-scenarios.R`) for two
levels of vaccination coverage: none (R0 = `r p$R0` in a fully susceptible
city) and `r 100 * res[[2]]$params$prop_vaccinated`% (effective R ≈
`r fmt(p$R0 * (1 - res[[2]]$params$prop_vaccinated * p$vax_efficacy), 1)`).
Each simulation starts from a single introduction. Summaries only include
runs in which the baseline produced an outbreak (50 or more infections), and
the "Outbreaks" column gives their share. "Infected at trigger" and
"Reported at trigger" are medians on the trigger day.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-summary
#| echo: false
tab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(cov) {
  x <- copy(res[[cov]]$summary)
  x[, coverage := paste0(100 * as.numeric(cov), "%")]
  x[, ww_threshold := fmt(res[[cov]]$calibration$threshold, 1)]
  x
}))
trig <- function(x, scenario) ifelse(scenario == "baseline", "", fmt(x))
tab[, .(
  Coverage                       = coverage,
  `Outbreaks (%)`                = fmt(pct_outbreak),
  Scenario                       = scenario,
  `WW threshold (copies/mL)`     = ifelse(
    scenario == "wastewater",
    ww_threshold,
    ""
  ),
  `Trigger day`                  = trig(trigger_day, scenario),
  `Infected at trigger`          = trig(infected_at_trigger, scenario),
  `Reported at trigger`          = trig(reported_at_trigger, scenario),
  `Infections, median [IQR]`     = sprintf(
    "%s [%s, %s]",
    fmt(final_size),
    fmt(final_q25),
    fmt(final_q75)
  ),
  `Averted vs baseline, mean`    = trig(averted, scenario),
  `Lead of WW over cases (days)` = ifelse(
    scenario == "wastewater",
    fmt(lead_median),
    ""
  )
)] |> knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Mean daily new infections by scenario."
curves <- rbindlist(lapply(res, `[[`, "curves"))
curves[, coverage := paste0("Vaccination coverage: ", 100 * coverage, "%")]
ggplot(curves, aes(day, new_inf, colour = scenario)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~coverage, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "New infections (mean)", colour = "Scenario") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 200)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: takeaway-values
#| include: false
get <- function(cov, sc, v) res[[cov]]$summary[scenario == sc][[v]]
p85 <- res[["0.85"]]$params
r85 <- p$R0 * (1 - p85$prop_vaccinated * p85$vax_efficacy)
```

### Takeaways

- **Without vaccination**, WW triggers a median of
  `r fmt(get("0", "wastewater", "lead_median"))` days before the case-based
  trigger. At that point about `r fmt(get("0", "wastewater", "infected_at_trigger"))`
  people are infected and `r fmt(get("0", "wastewater", "reported_at_trigger"))`
  cases have been reported. The case trigger fires at about
  `r fmt(get("0", "cases", "infected_at_trigger"))` infected and
  `r fmt(get("0", "cases", "reported_at_trigger"))` reported. Both thresholds
  respond to the same number of cases (about
  `r fmt(res[["0"]]$calibration$target)`); WW simply sees them earlier.
  However, the school-age intervention only lowers R from `r p$R0` to about
  `r fmt(res[["0"]]$R_int, 1)`, so neither trigger stops a city-wide
  outbreak.
- **With `r 100 * p85$prop_vaccinated`% coverage** (effective R ≈
  `r fmt(r85, 1)`), the same intervention brings R just below one (≈
  `r fmt(r85 * res[["0.85"]]$R_int / p$R0, 2)`) and averts most infections.
  But the outbreak grows slowly, and at `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`%
  case detection the WW lead is about
  `r fmt(get("0.85", "wastewater", "lead_median"))` days, so the
  differences between the WW and case-based scenarios are within
  simulation noise. WW gains a clear advantage only when clinical
  detection is lower (see
  [Case detection probability](#case-detection-probability)).
- The WW lead comes from shedding during the prodrome (about 4 days before
  rash) plus the case-reporting delay, minus the lab turnaround. Each extra
  day of turnaround removes about one day of lead. With a 7-day turnaround,
  the median lead is `r fmt(res[["0"]]$lab_delay[ww_lab_delay == 7, lead_median])`
  days without vaccination and
  `r fmt(res[["0.85"]]$lab_delay[ww_lab_delay == 7, lead_median])` days with
  `r 100 * p85$prop_vaccinated`% coverage (table below).
- Earlier detection pays off most when the outbreak grows fast *and* the
  triggered intervention is strong enough to bring R below one. With
  R0 = `r p$R0` and no vaccination, that would take broader measures than
  reducing school-age contacts.

### Lab turnaround time

The value of earlier detection shrinks as the lab turnaround time grows. Here
the WW threshold is fixed at its calibrated value:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lab
#| echo: false
lab <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(cov) {
  x <- copy(res[[cov]]$lab_delay)
  x[, coverage := paste0(100 * as.numeric(cov), "%")]
  x
}))
lab[, .(
  Coverage                      = coverage,
  `Lab turnaround (days)`       = ww_lab_delay,
  `Trigger day`                 = fmt(trigger_day),
  `Lead of WW over cases (days)` = fmt(lead_median),
  `Infections averted, mean`    = fmt(averted)
)] |> knitr::kable()
```

### Case detection probability

Measles cases are hard to detect clinically: many are never seen by a
clinician, tested, or reported. Here each case is detected during its rash
period with a given probability, and the WW threshold stays at the value
calibrated for `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`% detection. WW does not depend on
clinical detection, so only the case-based trigger changes. Case detection
uses common random numbers (one draw per case), so the cases detected at a
lower probability are a subset of those detected at a higher one, and the
lead is paired with the same WW runs. "Triggered" is the share of outbreaks
in which the case-based trigger fired; the lead is computed over outbreaks
in which both triggers fired.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-report
#| echo: false
rp <- rbindlist(lapply(names(res), function(cov) {
  x <- copy(res[[cov]]$report_prob)
  x[, coverage := paste0(100 * as.numeric(cov), "%")]
  x
}))
setorder(rp, coverage, -case_report_prob)
rp[, .(
  Coverage                       = coverage,
  `Case detection (%)`           = fmt(100 * case_report_prob),
  `Triggered (%)`                = fmt(pct_trigger),
  `Trigger day`                  = fmt(trigger_day),
  `Infected at trigger`          = fmt(infected_at_trigger),
  `Lead of WW over cases (days)` = fmt(lead_median),
  `Infections averted, mean`     = fmt(averted)
)] |> knitr::kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: report-values
#| include: false
rget <- function(cov, prob, v)
  res[[cov]]$report_prob[case_report_prob == prob][[v]]
rmin <- min(res[["0"]]$report_prob$case_report_prob)
```

- Lower clinical detection delays the case-based trigger, so the WW lead
  grows: without vaccination it goes from
  `r fmt(rget("0", p$case_report_prob, "lead_median"))` days at
  `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`% detection to
  `r fmt(rget("0", rmin, "lead_median"))` days at `r 100 * rmin`%.
- With `r 100 * p85$prop_vaccinated`% coverage the outbreak grows slowly,
  so missed cases cost more time: the lead goes from
  `r fmt(rget("0.85", p$case_report_prob, "lead_median"))` days at
  `r 100 * p$case_report_prob`% detection to
  `r fmt(rget("0.85", rmin, "lead_median"))` days at `r 100 * rmin`%, and
  the infections averted by the case-based trigger fall from
  `r fmt(rget("0.85", p$case_report_prob, "averted"))` to
  `r fmt(rget("0.85", rmin, "averted"))` (WW:
  `r fmt(get("0.85", "wastewater", "averted"))`).
- Without vaccination the averted infections barely change, because the
  intervention cannot stop the outbreak regardless of when it starts.

The grid of detection probabilities is set by `report_probs` (and the
reference value by `report_prob_ref`) in `analysis/run-scenarios.R`.

## Reproducing

The analysis needs epiworldR 0.19.0, measles 0.4.1, and multigroup.vaccine
0.1.1, which are installed from GitHub at pinned commits. The easiest way to
get them is the dev container (`.devcontainer/Containerfile`), which also pins
the R version and the CRAN snapshot:

- **In the browser**:
  [![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)](https://codespaces.new/EpiForeSITE/wastewater-econ-abm?devcontainer_path=.devcontainer/web/devcontainer.json)
  (uses `.devcontainer/web/devcontainer.json`).
- **Locally**: open the project in VS Code with the Dev Containers extension
  (uses `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json`), or build the image directly with
  `docker build -f .devcontainer/Containerfile .devcontainer`.

The image is built and tested by the `Dev container` GitHub Actions workflow,
and published as `ghcr.io/epiforesite/wastewater-econ-abm-dev` from `main`.
Inside the container:

```r
source("analysis/run-scenarios.R")   # writes analysis/results.rds
quarto::quarto_render("README.qmd")
tinytest::run_test_dir("tests")
```

All parameters are set in `measles_ww_params()` (R/simulate.R) and can be
changed, e.g., `measles_ww_params(R0 = 12, ww_lab_delay = 5)`.

- Genotype-specific detection of measles virus using wastewater surveillance,

- Wastewater surveillance for measles virus during a measles outbreak,
